Check old-age mortality models out of sample

Source: R/derive-oldage.R
mt_open_check.Rd

Fits the hazard laws of life_table() to the deaths at ages from to cut - 1 and scores their extrapolation against the observed deaths at ages cut and above, the design of Thatcher, Kannisto and Vaupel (1998, chapter 6): they fit six models at ages 80-98 and compare the predicted probabilities of dying with the observed ones at ages 99 and over. The predictions are based only on the data below the cut, so they are independent of the observations they are compared with.

Usage

mt_open_check(
  data,
  cut = 99,
  from = 80,
  to = NULL,
  laws = c("gompertz", "kannisto", "makeham", "weibull", "beard", "logquad", "logistic",
    "perks", "lynch_brown"),
  by_age = FALSE
)

Arguments

data

An mt_data object with deaths and exposures in single years of age from from to to.

cut

First age of the test ages; the laws are fitted to the ages from to cut - 1 (Thatcher et al. 1998: 99, fitting ages 80-98).

from

First age of the fit (default 80, the lowest age of the data of Thatcher et al.).

to

Last test age (default: the last single year of age of the data).

laws

Hazard laws to check, see life_table() (default: all nine models of Feehan 2018).

by_age

Return one row per test age instead of the sums.

Value

A data.table with the stratum columns, period and law, n_par (number of parameters), loglik, aic and delta_aic of the fit, the out-of-sample sums nll and chisq over n_ages test ages, rank (by nll within each stratum and period, 1 = best) and converged. With by_age = TRUE, one row per test age with age, N, d, the observed q_obs = d / N, the predicted q_fit, nll and chisq. No thresholds: the check shows which law extrapolated best in these data.

Details

Every law is fitted by maximum likelihood with binomial deaths: of the N_x persons who reach age x, d_x die before x + 1 with probability q_x = 1 - exp(-H_x), where H_x is the integral of the hazard over the year (Thatcher et al. 1998, chapter 6; Feehan 2018, equation 4). The deaths are those of the data and N = E + d / 2, the person-years E plus half the deaths, as for life_table() with exposure (Thatcher et al. use the numbers reaching each age directly). At the test ages, with the predicted q, Thatcher et al. compare the models by

  • nll: minus the binomial log-likelihood of the observed deaths, -(d log q + (N - d) log(1 - q)), without the binomial coefficients, which are the same for all models (their Table 6.3); the model with the lowest sum fits best on the likelihood criterion (rank);

  • chisq: (d - N q)^2 / (N q (1 - q)), distributed like chi-squared with one degree of freedom per age for a correct model and accurate data (their Table 6.4), so that the sum over n_ages ages has expected value n_ages.

The columns aic and delta_aic give Akaike's information criterion of the fit below the cut, -2 loglik + 2 k with k parameters, and its difference to the lowest value of the schedule, as Feehan (2018, section 4.2) compares the models; without the binomial coefficients, which cancel in the differences. Thatcher et al. pool the data of decades and 13 countries: pool periods with mt_regroup() (period = ) before the check. Cells whose deaths exceed the numbers at risk (d > N, possible for period data with tiny exposures) are left out (package-specific safeguard).

References

Feehan DM (2018). Separating the signal from the noise: evidence for deceleration in old-age death rates. Demography 55(6): 2025-2044. doi:10.1007/s13524-018-0728-x

Thatcher AR, Kannisto V, Vaupel JW (1998). The Force of Mortality at Ages 80 to 120. Odense University Press.

See also

life_table() for the laws and their use as a closure of the open age interval.

Examples

# expected deaths of a cohort under a Kannisto hazard: the laws fitted at
# 80-94 are scored at ages 95-104
x <- 80:104
H <- log1p(5e-5 * exp(0.11 * (x + 1))) / 0.11 - log1p(5e-5 * exp(0.11 * x)) / 0.11
N <- 1e5 * exp(-cumsum(c(0, H[-length(H)])))
d <- round(N * (1 - exp(-H)))
sim <- mt_data(deaths = data.frame(age = x, year = 2000, deaths = d),
               exposure = data.frame(age = x, year = 2000, exposure = N - d / 2))
chk <- mt_open_check(sim, cut = 95, laws = c("gompertz", "kannisto", "logquad", "beard"))
chk[, list(law, nll, chisq, n_ages, rank)]
#>         law      nll    chisq n_ages  rank
#>      <char>    <num>    <num>  <num> <int>
#> 1: gompertz 212.7159 8.625589      9     4
#> 2: kannisto 209.1797 1.061330      9     1
#> 3:  logquad 209.1924 1.087074      9     3
#> 4:    beard 209.1810 1.063967      9     2
